text: Vitruvius describes a Roman water-lifting drum divided into eight compartments. Workers tread it round so water enters at the rim and exits near the axle into a trough: it moves a large volume but does not lift it very high (Book X.4).
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Vitruvius, De architectura, Augustan Roman world, translated by Morris Hicky Morgan (1914), public-domain primary text; https://www.gutenberg.org/files/20239/20239-h/20239-h.htm . Verified primary context: Book X.4.1-2; chapter also specified in the stimulus.

text: For a greater lifting height, Vitruvius describes bronze buckets on a double iron chain running around an axle. Each bucket tips its water into a reservoir as it passes over the top, turning intermittent scoops into a continuous supply (Book X.4).
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Vitruvius, De architectura, Augustan Roman world, translated by Morris Hicky Morgan (1914), public-domain primary text; https://www.gutenberg.org/files/20239/20239-h/20239-h.htm . Verified primary context: Book X.4.4; chapter also specified in the stimulus.

text: Vitruvius describes floatboards attached to a wheel so that a river current turns it and raises water in boxes. In his Augustan Roman account, the current supplies motion that a tread-powered lifting wheel otherwise gets from workers (Book X.5).
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Vitruvius, De architectura, Augustan Roman world, translated by Morris Hicky Morgan (1914), public-domain primary text; https://www.gutenberg.org/files/20239/20239-h/20239-h.htm . Verified primary context: Book X.5.1; chapter also specified in the stimulus.
